chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
title: Staying on the bandstand at white dances, and playing Dixie
summary: Rules of not mingling at white dances, how he felt, and insisting his band play Dixie.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You were careful not to talk to anybody?

People could come ask us things, but you just didn't go out there and touch, or talk, or mingle, or nothing. And like I said, when you come off the bandstand, you walk side the bandstand. You don't go out, you walk side the bandstand, round down to the bathroom.
But you'd see all of that, you know, even then. How'd you feel about that, having to?

I didn't have any feeling towards that. You know, I can't say what it was I felt, but I have never been the way that some people were. You know, to me, kind of, you know, you're out there searching for something. Okay, I just felt I'm me. Here I am, accept me as I am. I ain't giving you no trouble, you don't give me nothing. That's all. Now there's one song that we used to play. The band, fellas in the band didn't like to play it, but I played it, and I made them play it. It was Dixie. See, we can play at LSU Baton Rouge, anywhere in the south, you have to play Dixie. I don't play it. I said, Dixie's a song, what Dixie going to do to you? And they got mad with me, but I played Dixie. And they'll tell you about it, I'll play Dixie. And I kept playing it with you. It's the final, that was the final.
